message:
fix(update): the host was waiting on the bootstrap, which is supposed to exit

The process the host starts copies the updater aside, launches that copy
and exits at once -- it has to, because the file it is running from is one
of the files the update replaces. The host was watching that process and
reading its exit as the updater having died. So on the ordinary path it
told the user the installed version was unchanged, closed the ready event
and stopped listening, while the working copy was still downloading. The
copy then signalled into an event nobody held, did not look at whether the
signal was delivered, and stopped the host it had just been promised would
be left alone.

A remote user is told the update was cancelled, and then loses the
machine. Every part of this was individually correct.

The wait has a third answer now: keep waiting. A bootstrap that exits zero
handed over, and one that exits non-zero failed before there was anything
to wait for -- so the exit code is read, and an unreadable one counts as
failure rather than being mistaken for a deliberate handover.

The handshake has a second direction. Signalling ready tells the host
something; it does not tell the updater that anyone heard. The host
acknowledges only when it is actually standing down, the updater waits for
that answer before it stops anything, and signalReady returns whether it
was delivered at all. Delivered-but-unanswered and never-delivered are
distinct, because a host that has already told the user "no update today"
must not then be shut down by a late arrival.

The wait itself moved out of the lambda it was written in. It could only
be run by performing a real update against the real product, so it was
never run, and that is how it stayed wrong. The regression starts a real
bootstrap and a real worker and calls await_handoff -- the function the
product calls, not a reproduction of it. Reverting the rule makes the
ordinary-update case fail and the race sweep never reach ExitNow at all:
with the old logic no update completes.
